title: Data that arrives by the clock: storing time series
dek: Rider speeds every 10 seconds, orders per minute per city, the latency of every API: data that arrives in time order, is read by time range, and matters less as it ages. Here is why general databases struggle with it, how time-series stores compress and expire it, and the one mistake that sinks them: too many series.

items: It is written in time order, almost never updated, and arrives fast: 2 lakh riders reporting every 10 seconds is 20,000 points a second.
It is read by range and summarised: 'average speed per 5 minutes in Pune over the last hour', 'p99 latency today'.
Its value fades: last hour in full detail, last year as hourly summaries, and older than that, not at all.
A general database can do it, but one row per point with indexes wastes space and makes deleting old data a heavy job.

body.x: How time-series stores keep it small

body.cap: Points from one series are similar to their neighbours, so storing only what changed shrinks them about tenfold.

items: Each series' points are kept together, so reading one series over an hour reads one block, not points scattered among others.
Old data is removed by dropping whole blocks, which is instant compared with deleting crores of rows.
Compression of times (delta of delta) and values (XOR with the previous value) brings a point from 16 bytes to around 1.4 in typical monitoring data.

body.x: Keeping less detail as data ages

body.cap: Dashboards rarely need ten-second detail from last year. Summaries keep the shape of old data at a fraction of the cost.

items: Store summaries (minimum, maximum, sum, count) rather than only averages, so the average over a longer window can still be computed correctly.
Percentiles can't be averaged. Keep a histogram or a sketch per interval and merge those instead.
Decide retention per metric: business numbers for years, debugging detail for days.
A series is a metric plus a set of label values: orders_placed{city=pune, app=android} is one series; changing any label makes another.
Labels should have few values: city, app version, status. Each label multiplies the number of series by its number of values.
Never put an ID in a label (order_id, user_id, request_id). It makes a series per ID, each with one point, and the index of series grows until the store falls over. Put IDs in logs or traces instead.
Check with arithmetic: 30 cities × 5 app versions × 4 statuses is 600 series; adding user_id with 1 crore users is 600 crore.

body.label: TWO WAYS TO ASK FOR ORDERS PER MINUTE
body.x:
# PromQL (Prometheus): orders a second, per city, over 5-minute windows
sum by (city) (rate(orders_placed_total[5m]))

-- TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL): average rider speed per 5 minutes, last hour
SELECT time_bucket('5 minutes', at) AS t, avg(kmph)
FROM rider_speed
WHERE at > now() - interval '1 hour'
GROUP BY t ORDER BY t;
body.say: Two queries. In Prometheus, the rate of the orders placed counter over 5-minute windows, summed per city. In TimescaleDB, average rider speed in 5-minute buckets over the last hour.

items: Name it as time series when data is append-only, time-ordered and read by range: metrics, sensor readings, location trails.
Give the write rate (sources × frequency) and retention, then the storage after compression.
Plan rollups for old data and say which store you'd use.
Watch cardinality: list the labels and multiply.
Where it appears here: the Ad clicks problem stores counts per ad per minute, a time series built by a stream job.

body.label: Go deeper: why counters, not gauges, for rates

body.x: A counter only goes up (orders placed since the server started); a gauge goes up and down (riders online now). To chart orders per minute, store the counter and let the query compute the rate between samples. If a sample is missed, the next one still contains every order, so nothing is lost; a stored 'orders this minute' value that is missed is simply gone. Rate functions also handle the counter resetting to zero when a server restarts.
